newsitem.title: FRANCE: Sons of French defence minister fight spy charge.
newsitem.headline: Sons of French defence minister fight spy charge.

text.p: The sons of Charles Hernu, the late Socialist defence minister, urged a French court on Thursday to order a magazine to pay 30 million francs ($6 million) in damages for reporting that their father spied for the communist bloc.

The weekly L'Express published documents in October and January purporting to show that Hernu, under the codename "Andre", had been a Soviet, Romanian and Bulgarian agent in the 1950s and 1960s. Hernu, defence minister from 1981 to 1985, died in 1990.

According to the magazine, Hernu was paid for supplying general information on French politics and other subjects. In 1958 he reportedly told the Soviet ambasssador in Paris the size of the French army fighting rebels in Algeria.

Public prosecutor Fabienne Goget said at the hearing that "the court's task is not to write history but to say whether there any faults in the work of L'Express". She said it was up to Hernu's family to prove damages existed.

Serge Lewisch, the lawyer representing Hernu sons Jean-Michel, Jean-Charles and Patrice, said the documents published by L'Express may be fake, and that they had been mistakenly translated by the magazine.

"These documents are more than dubious...Even if they are true, which has yet to be demonstrated, publication and translation of these texts was not done in an honest manner," Lewisch said, stressing that the information allegedly supplied by Hernu was of little importance.
Patrice Hernu denounced what he called a manipulation and said the documents were fakes.
Francis Szpiner, lawyer for L'Express, said the weekly had contributed to the history of "the fascination of French politicians and intellectuals for the Eastern European countries".

He said L'Express had established that "the revelations made by Charles Hernu constitute intelligence to the enemy". Their slight strategic nature was of little importance, he said. What mattered was the source.
L'Express has said it was not clear whether Hernu had maintained relations with Soviet services after 1963.

In other documents dated 1957-58 and purported to come from the archives of the Soviet Foreign Ministry, a diplomat named as Vladimir Yerofeyev and former Soviet ambassador to France Sergei Vinogradov recounted lunch conversations with Hernu in memoranda addressed directly to then foreign minister Andrei Gromyko.
L'Express said Hernu had disclosed the address of U.S. secret services in Paris and had given analyses and forecasts of French politics.

L'Express said in November that France's DST counter-intelligence service had informed the late president Francois Mitterrand, Hernu's political patron, in 1992 after it received a dossier from east European spy services.
It said the DST had been unable to verify the charges and Mitterrand had ordered the reports to be kept secret, arguing Hernu could not defend himself.
